food.text: The Great Famine of 1876–1878 killed between 5.6 and 10.3 million people. The toll was large enough to offset the usual population growth in the Bombay and Madras Presidencies between the censuses of 1871 and 1881. Droughts combined with policy failures repeatedly turned failed harvests into catastrophe.

In the 19th century Indian cooks simplified and adjusted curries for their British masters. Curry became "a dish in its own right, created for the British in India", but it was eaten only by the British. Indians named their dishes specifically, while the British lumped them together as curry.

Indian Chinese cuisine began in the 19th century among the Chinese community of Calcutta. Hakka Chinese from Canton came to escape the First and Second Opium Wars and political instability. Meeting local food, they added Indian spices and cooking techniques to their own, creating a fusion of the two.

Anglo-Indian cuisine took shape when British wives, or memsahibs, told Indian cooks what food they wanted, transforming many dishes. In the late 18th and early 19th centuries, when few British women were in India, British men often lived with Indian mistresses and picked up local food, language and customs.

Colonel Arthur Robert Kenney-Herbert, writing as "Wyvern", documented Anglo-Indian cooking in practical detail in his 1878 Culinary Jottings for Madras. Many of its terms were later described in Hobson-Jobson, the Anglo-Indian dictionary of 1886.

The Great Famine of 1876–1878 sent many agricultural laborers and artisans from southern India to British tropical colonies. There they worked as indentured labourers on plantations. Hunger at home thus pushed people overseas.

A quarama from Lucknow contained ghee, yoghurt, cream, crushed almonds, cloves, cardamom and saffron. An 1869 Anglo-Indian quorema, or korma, had no cream, almonds or saffron. It added the standard British curry spices: coriander, ginger and black peppercorns.

The Odisha famine of 1866–1867 later spread through the Madras Presidency to Hyderabad and Mysore. About a third of Odisha's population died. In Odisha the British Secretary of State for India, Lord Salisbury, did nothing for two months, by which time a million people had died. The famine left an estimated 1,553 orphans, whose guardians were to receive 3 rupees per month until the child reached 17 for boys and 16 for girls.

Indian food travelled abroad in the 19th century. Indentured Indian sugar workers carried curry to the Caribbean, while British traders took it to Japan. Together these journeys helped make curry an international dish.

Hyderabad has long drawn migrants from across the Indian subcontinent and beyond, particularly since 1857. Foreign dishes were adapted to local tastes. Persian dried lamb with beans was modified with dalcha, and the Uzbek tandoori naan was reworked into sheermal.

Hobson-Jobson defined pish pash as "a slop of rice-soup with small pieces of meat in it, much used in the Anglo-Indian nursery". Augustus Prinsep first recorded the term in the mid 19th century. The name may come from the Persian pash-pash, from pashidan, to break.

art.text: The Government College of Art & Craft in Kolkata is one of the oldest art colleges in India. It was founded on 16 August 1854 as the School of Industrial Art, meant to teach youth of all classes industrial art based on scientific methods.

Indo-Saracenic architecture was a revivalist style used mostly by British architects in India in the late 19th century. It was applied to public and government buildings and to the palaces of princely state rulers, borrowing from Indo-Islamic and especially Mughal architecture, which the British regarded as the classic Indian style.

The Tanjore school of painting, named after the town of Tanjavur in Tamil Nadu, uses real gold and silver foil, semiprecious stones, beads, mirrors and powdered metals. Artists also used the primary colours red, green, blue, black and white to depict key figures.

The Bengal school of art emerged from efforts to reform teaching at the Government School of Art in Kolkata. Ernest Binfield Havel, principal from 1896 to 1905, tried to emphasise Indian traditions in the curriculum, and this led to the emergence of the style known as the Bengal school.

Abanindranath Tagore served as Vice-Principal of the Kolkata art college from 15 August 1905 to 1915. He worked towards developing an Indian style of art, which gave birth to the Bengal school of art, an agenda later pursued at Kala Bhavan, Shantiniketan.

Indo-Saracenic style drew on Western exposure to depictions of Indian buildings from about 1795, such as those by William Hodges and the Daniell duo, William Daniell and his uncle Thomas Daniell. Bombay and Calcutta, as the main centres of Raj administration, saw many buildings built in the style.
The Bengal school countered the values of the academic realists in Indian art. It is strongly represented by Abanindranath Tagore and his followers M. A. R Chughtai and Kshitindra Majumdar.

Italianate architecture, popularised in early Victorian Britain, was adopted in India in the later parts of the 19th century. The one outstanding building in this class was the East Indian Railway Head Offices at Calcutta, built in 1884.

Neoclassical buildings in India include St Andrews Church in Madras (1821), Raj Bhawan (1803) and Metcalfe Hall (1844) in Kolkata, as well as Falaknuma Palace (1893) in Hyderabad. Some large private houses in and around Kolkata were built in this style by wealthy merchants.

In 1877 a severe famine struck the Tinnevelly District and thousands of people died, leaving a large number of destitute children orphaned and without their parents. In 1878 Arthur Margoschis started an orphanage, St. John's Orphanage, to give them food and shelter; it later became the Art Industrial School in Nazareth, Tamil Nadu. By 1900 it housed 283 inmates and offered technical training in 18 trades, including carving, weaving, dyeing, lace making and embroidery.

The Mysore school of painting sprang up in south Karnataka during the reign of Maharaja Mummudi Krishnaraja Wadiyar. It presents a wide variety, from murals to stylistic paintings on cloth, paper and wood.

The National Museum of India displays Tanjore paintings from the early 19th century, including Navaneeta Krishna with Tanjore King Shivaji II (1830 CE) and the Durbar of Serfoji II (1798 to 1833). Among them is also Nataraja Shiva, from the early 19th century.

war.text: The Indian Rebellion of 1857 began on 10 May 1857 as a mutiny of sepoys of the East India Company's garrison in Meerut, a town 40 miles northeast of Delhi. That evening the rebels killed British junior officers who tried to quell the outbreak, attacked officers' and civilians' quarters, and killed four civilian men, eight women and eight children; about 50 Indian civilians, some of them servants who tried to defend or hide their employers, were also killed. It spread into other mutinies and civilian rebellions, chiefly in the upper Gangetic plain and central India, and threatened British power there.

By the eve of the 1857 rebellion, the East India Company controlled most of the Indian subcontinent, directly or indirectly. It had expanded through wars such as the Second Anglo-Sikh War, after which it annexed the Punjab in 1849, and it annexed the kingdom of Oudh in 1856 on grounds of alleged misgovernment.

The 1857 rebellion was fed by resentment of invasive British-style social reforms, harsh land taxes, and the summary treatment of some rich landowners and princes. Rebels also doubted British claims that their rule brought material improvement to the Indian economy.

After the crushing defeat of the war of 1857 to 1858, which he nominally led, the last Mughal, Bahadur Shah Zafar, was deposed and exiled by the East India Company in 1858 to Rangoon, Burma. Before that, on 20 September 1857, Major William Hodson's Company forces surrounded Humayun's Tomb, where Zafar had taken refuge, and captured him. The next day Hodson shot Zafar's sons Mirza Mughal and Mirza Khizr Sultan and his grandson Mirza Abu Bakht on his own authority at the Khooni Darwaza. His wife Zeenat Mahal and some other family members accompanied him into exile.

The First Anglo-Sikh War of 1845 to 1846 ended with the Treaty of Lahore, under which the Sikhs surrendered the Jullundur Doab and owed an indemnity of 1.2 million rupees. Unable to pay, they saw the Company let Gulab Singh acquire Kashmir for 750,000 rupees, and he became its first maharaja.

Following the Anglo-Nepalese War of 1814 to 1816, Nepal stayed independent but accepted a treaty that set up a British resident. It also began a close military relationship, including the recruitment of Gurkha soldiers into British service.

The British began to gain ground again from the end of 1857 and retook Lucknow in March 1858. The last rebels were defeated in Gwalior on 20 June 1858, and by 1859 rebel leaders Bakht Khan and Nana Sahib had either been slain or had fled. The fighting was marked by exceptional cruelty on both sides: rebels killed British officers and civilians, including women and children, while British reprisals fell on rebels and their supporters, sometimes entire villages, and Delhi and Lucknow were laid waste in the fighting and the retaliation.
At 4 am on 7 October 1858, Bahadur Shah Zafar began his journey to Rangoon with his wives and two remaining sons. They travelled in bullock carts escorted by the 9th Lancers under Lieutenant Ommaney.

In 1804, Mughal forces under Shah Alam II, allied with the East India Company, faced Maratha forces at Delhi, which the Marathas had lost to the Company in 1803. Yashwantrao Holkar confronted the British commander David Ochterlony but abandoned the siege when reinforcements led by Gerard Lake arrived on 18 October.

After the rebellion, the British granted amnesty on 1 November 1858 to all rebels not involved in murder. They did not declare hostilities formally ended until 8 July 1859. Among the killings was the Bibighar massacre at Cawnpore, where five men and 206 women and children were held hostage and 25 died of dysentery and cholera in a week. After a Company relief force defeated the Indians, two Muslim butchers, two Hindu peasants and one of Nana Sahib's bodyguards went in armed with knives and hatchets and murdered the women and children; the dead and dying were thrown down a well.

The Indian Order of Merit was introduced by the East India Company in 1837 and taken over by the Crown in 1858 after the Mutiny of 1857. Between 1837 and 1907 it was the only gallantry medal available to Native soldiers.

British India gained a common border with Tibet in 1826, after the British took Manipur and Assam from the Burmese following the First Anglo-Burmese War of 1824 to 1826. This war helped lay the ground for later border disputes with Tibet and China.

literature.text: Sangam literature, the earliest known literature of South India, was lost and forgotten for most of the second millennium. Colonial-era scholars rediscovered it in the late nineteenth century, in Hindu monasteries near Kumbakonam.

In 1913, the Bengali poet Rabindranath Tagore became India's first Nobel laureate in literature. He received the Nobel Prize for his work "Gitanjali", and he was also the first Asian to win the Nobel Prize.

Arumuka Navalar of Jaffna first inaugurated the modern editions of Tamil classics. He published a fine edition of the Tirukkuṟaḷ by 1860, at a time when much of the older Tamil literature had been forgotten.

Arumuka Navalar translated the Bible into Tamil while working as an assistant to a Methodist Christian missionary. He then chose to defend Shaiva Hinduism against missionary polemics, in part by bringing ancient Tamil and Shaiva literature to wider attention.

The Charyapada, Buddhist hymns from the 8th century, are the oldest known written form of Bengali. The Bengali linguist Hara Prasad Shastri discovered the palm leaf manuscript in the Nepal Royal Court Library in 1907.
Arumuka Navalar brought the first Sangam text into print in 1851. It was the Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai, one of the Ten Idylls.

Navalar and other colonial-era scholars, including C.W. Damodaram Pillai and U. V. Swaminatha Aiyar, printed Kalittokai in 1887, Silappatikaram in 1889 and Manimekalai in 1898. Together they published more than 100 works in all, including minor poems.
In 1868, Arumuka Navalar published an early commentary on the Tolkappiyam, an ancient Tamil work. It was part of his effort to bring Tamil classics back into print.

The same scholars also printed Pattuppāṭṭu and Patiṟṟuppattu in 1889, Puṟanāṉūṟu in 1894 and Aiṅkurunūṟu in 1903, all with scholarly commentaries. Each printed volume returned a piece of the Sangam corpus to readers.

science.text: Throughout most of the 19th century, the Survey of India carried out the Great Trigonometric Survey. To reach the highest accuracy, a number of corrections were applied to all distances calculated from simple trigonometry.

Photography spread to India at a fast pace after the daguerreotype was invented and publicized in 1839. By 1840, advertisements for imported cameras placed by Thacker, Spink & Co. were appearing in Calcutta in a periodical titled Friends of India.

The Great Trigonometric Survey was piloted in its early stages by William Lambton and later by George Everest. It was a project of the Survey of India, which the British East India Company had established in 1767.

The earliest known surviving photographic capture in India dates to 1840. It is a lithograph based on a daguerreotype of the Sans Souci Theatre in Calcutta. By the later 1840s, the first known commercial photographic studio was operating in Calcutta.
Photographic societies sprang up in Bombay in 1854, and in Calcutta and Madras in 1856. They aimed to spread awareness and understanding of photography by holding meetings and annual exhibitions.

John McCosh, a British military surgeon employed by the East India Company, photographed the Second Anglo-Sikh War of 1848 to 1849. Using calotype technology, he made some of the earliest known examples of war photography in history, including images of people and places in Lahore.

In 1848, McCosh took a portrait of the reigning 10-year-old Maharaja Duleep Singh of the Sikh Empire, seated on a chair in a profile pose. He also made images of Bikram Singh Bedi, Maharani Jind Kaur, and Diwan Mulraj.
Charles Waterloo Hutchinson was one of the earliest photographers of the Golden Temple in Amritsar. He recorded a photo of the site in 1856, around seven years after the fall of the Sikh Empire.

The Italian-British photographer Felice Beato traveled the northern regions of the subcontinent after the Indian Mutiny of 1857. He photographed Akali-Nihangs, Sikh soldiers in Hodson's Horse, and views of the Golden Temple complex in Amritsar.

Many photographers and studios captured the Golden Temple and other Sikh sites between the 19th and early 20th centuries. They included Samuel Bourne in 1863 to 1865, Bourne & Shepherd in the 1880s and 1890s, and Herbert G. Ponting and Hannah P. Adams, both in 1906.

politics.text: On 28 June 1858, after the Indian Rebellion of 1857, the rule of the East India Company was transferred to the Crown in the person of Queen Victoria. This began the period of British Raj, or Crown rule, which lasted until 1947. In 1876 Victoria was proclaimed Empress of India.

The British Raj included areas directly run by the United Kingdom, called British India, and areas ruled by indigenous rulers under British paramountcy, called the princely states. The whole region was commonly called India, and was sometimes called the Indian Empire, though not officially.

The East India Company expanded its power partly by outright annexation of Indian states. Annexed regions included the North-Western Provinces in 1801, Delhi in 1803, Assam in 1828 and Sindh in 1843. Punjab, the North-West Frontier Province and Kashmir followed after the Anglo-Sikh Wars.

In 1905 Viceroy Lord Curzon split the Bengal Presidency into the Muslim-majority province of Eastern Bengal and Assam and the Hindu-majority province of Bengal. Earlier colonial administrations had contemplated the partition of Bengal but never acted on it, and it transformed nationalist politics. Alongside the Swadeshi boycott of British goods, protesters sporadically took to political violence that included attacks on civilians, and young men in groups such as Jugantar bombed public buildings, staged armed robberies and assassinated British officials. The violence was ineffective, as most planned attacks were either prevented by the British or failed.

By the end of the 19th century, colonial governance of the sex trade had moved to legislative and biopolitical mechanisms of disease prevention within British military cantonments. The 1864 Cantonment Act provided for about twelve to fifteen Indian women per regiment of roughly a thousand British soldiers, kept in licensed brothels called chaklas and allowed to consort with soldiers only. It required their registration and mandatory medical examinations, and provided for building and extending hospitals in cantonments.

The last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, nominally led the Indian Rebellion of 1857. After a crushing defeat he was deposed on 21 September 1857, as Delhi came under siege by the East India Company. He was exiled in 1858 to Rangoon, Burma, and the Mughal Empire was formally dissolved.

In 1817 the British went to war with the Pindaris, raiders who had fled into Maratha territory. This quickly became the Third Anglo-Maratha War. By the end of 1818 the British had signed treaties with the Rajput states, offering protection from the Pindaris and Marathas, and Maratha influence in Rajasthan ended.

Overwhelmingly Hindu protest against the partition of Bengal led the Muslim elite in 1906 to ask the new viceroy, Lord Minto, for separate electorates for Muslims. This resulted in the founding of the All-India Muslim League in Dacca in December 1906. The League favored Curzon's partition plan.

Under the 1864 Cantonment Act, women working in chaklas were often required to be examined once a week for traces of venereal disease. Prostitutes were often confined against their wills in these prison hospitals, especially if found to have a venereal disease. Most of the women came from poor families with no other opportunities for social or economic independence, and the article says the structural inequalities that pushed women into prostitution were often enforced by the colonial governments.

Kashmir was annexed after the Anglo-Sikh Wars, which ran from 1849 to 1856 under the Marquess of Dalhousie as Governor General. It was immediately sold under the Treaty of Amritsar in 1850 to the Dogra dynasty of Jammu. Kashmir thereby became a princely state.

Most Rajput princes remained loyal to Britain during the Revolt of 1857. Few political changes were made in Rajputana until Indian independence in 1947. The Rajputana Agency held more than 20 princely states, the most notable being Udaipur, Jaipur, Bikaner and Jodhpur.

The Charter Act 1813 removed the East India Company's two hundred year old monopoly on most British trade with India. This forced the previously protected Indian market to open to British goods, which could be sold without Company tariffs or duties. Textile imports grew from £5.2 million in 1850 to £18.4 million in 1896.

The 1864 Cantonment Act was eventually extended to the Presidencies and Provinces of British India. When military personnel were increasingly struck down by venereal diseases, more regulations were demanded, leading to the Indian Contagious Disease Acts. These required registered women, who were often made to carry a license card, to undergo in-patient treatment if found infected, and those who refused could be imprisoned. None of these measures were applied to infected men. A further Cantonment Act in 1895 outlawed any licensing or official approval of prostitution in cantonments, though most of the military opposed it.

Curzon's wish to court the Muslims of East Bengal grew from British anxieties dating to the 1871 Census of British India, which first estimated populations in Muslim-majority regions. It also reflected the history of Muslims fighting the British in the 1857 Rebellion and the Second Anglo-Afghan War.

The 1864 Cantonment Act regulated prostitution on British military bases, with about twelve to fifteen Indian women kept in licensed brothels called chaklas for each regiment of about a thousand soldiers. The women, mostly from poor families with no other opportunities, were required to undergo mandatory medical examinations, often weekly, for venereal disease. Prostitutes were often confined against their wills in prison hospitals, especially if found to have a venereal disease. The Act was eventually extended to the Presidencies and Provinces of British India.

philosophy.text: In response to colonialism and contact with Western philosophy, 19th-century Indians developed new ways of thinking now called Neo-Vedanta and Hindu modernism. Their ideas centered on the universality of Indian philosophy, especially Vedanta, and on the unity of different religions.

Indian philosophy's modern period began roughly in 1800 and was shaped by encounters with Western thought. Philosophers tried to build comprehensive systems that could harmonize diverse philosophical and religious teachings.

Swami Vivekananda (1863-1902) used the teachings of Advaita Vedanta to argue that all the different religions are valid paths toward the one divine. This was a striking attempt to harmonize many religious traditions within a single philosophical framework.

The first of the Hindu modernist movements was the Brahmo Samaj of Ram Mohan Roy (1772-1833). It began the wave of reinterpretation that later thinkers built upon, and it was shaped in part by Western ideas.

Swami Vivekananda was very influential in developing the Hindu reform movements and in bringing their worldview to the West. Through Indians like him and Westerners such as the proponents of the Theosophical society, modern Hindu thought also influenced Western culture.

Beginning with Bankim Chandra Chatterjee in the nineteenth century, the word dharma took on a new meaning in modern Indian thought. It was presented as both an equivalent of and a response to the Western notion of religion, and the foreign tools of religion and nation became tools of self-definition.

The term Hinduism was developed in the 19th century by both Indian and European thinkers. The scholar Lorenzen locates the origins of a distinct Hindu identity in the interaction between Muslims and Hindus, a process of mutual self-definition that started well before 1800.

In April 1909, Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan was appointed to the Department of Philosophy at the Madras Presidency College. His philosophy was later grounded in Advaita Vedanta, which he reinterpreted for a contemporary understanding.

Buddhist modernism arose from engagement with the dominant cultural and intellectual forces of modernity, such as Enlightenment values and Western science. Important exponents included Anagarika Dharmapala (1864-1933) and the American convert Henry Steel Olcott.

Vivekananda (1863-1902) had a strong influence on the thought of Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan. Radhakrishnan gave intuition, which he also called religious experience, a central place in his philosophy as a source of knowledge not mediated by conscious thought.

culture.text: The British Raj brought the widespread introduction of the English language to India. This produced a local English dialect and also left its mark on other Indian languages.

Throughout the 19th century the British disarmed and demilitarized Indian society, and many Indians felt emasculated as a result. Bengalis in particular took up physical culture and martial arts to counter British stereotypes of effeteness, helped by organizations such as the Hindu Mela.

Western ideas of physical culture spread in India through groups such as the YMCA, and Indians hoped to gain from their scientific nature and European nationalistic vigor. Meanwhile the British tried to impose their own standards of physical discipline, discouraged traditional Indian games, and depicted Indian physiques negatively.

Indians used victory in sport as a way of proving themselves against the colonizer. They also worked to standardize and revitalize their native physical culture, with institutions such as the akharas and vyayamshalas playing a role.

The British government at first discouraged missionary work in India. In 1837 it allowed white missionaries into its territory because of pressure from the evangelical lobby in the British parliament.

In the nineteenth century, Bankim Chandra Chatterjee began a new use of dharma in modern Indian thought, presenting it as equivalent to, and a response to, the western notion of religion. Foreign tools such as religion and nation became tools of self-definition, and a new sense of the unity of Hinduism took root.

The poverty and starvation of the colonial period reduced Indians' ability to take part in physical exercise. This made the push for physical culture and martial arts, especially among Bengalis, all the more notable.

The Indian Government counted Jains as a major religious community right from the first census, conducted in 1873. This was long before independence in 1947, after which Jains were not treated as a national minority.
